Outcome: Depression cases (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: benefit
Claim: Working people with vitamin D deficiency had a higher prevalence of moderate depression than those with other vitamin D statuses.
Sentence: "The overall prevalence of moderate depression was 15%, with higher prevalence among working women compared to men [χ 2 (df) = 6.7(1), P=0.01], those practicing religions other than Hinduism [χ 2 (df) = 5.5(1), P=0.01], those educated up to primary school compared to other education criteria [χ 2 (df) = 9.4(4), P=0.03], those having vitamin D deficiency compared to others [χ 2 (df) = 8.5(3), P=0.03], and sedentary lifestyle compared to active lifestyle [χ 2 (df) = 6.7(1), P=0.009]."
Measured as: moderate depression (BDI-Ia score ≥20)
Population: Paid working population in Nepal (n=160)
Intervention: Vitamin D status (deficiency vs others), observed not given
Comparator: Participants without vitamin D deficiency
Design: cross-sectional study
Sample size: 160
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

## Study B
Found: no effect
Claim: Genetically lowered serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentrations were not associated with risk of major depression.
Sentence: "The odds ratio per genetically predicted one standard deviation decrease in S-25OHD concentrations was 1.02 (95% confidence interval 0.97⁻1.08; p = 0.44)."
Measured as: major depression
Population: Individuals of European ancestry from the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium (59,851 major depression cases and 113,154 controls)
Intervention: Genetically predicted serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentrations (six SNPs from SUNLIGHT)
Comparator: Per one standard deviation difference in genetically predicted S-25OHD
Design: other primary study
Sample size: 172,005
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported
